The Negev Desert. A triangular arid desert region comprising roughly forty-seven hundred square miles of southern Israel, extending southward from Beer Sheba to the Red Sea port of Eilat. Though harsh, it has supported Bedouin pastoralists and ancient settlements for millennia, and is central to modern Israeli history, economy, and national identity.

The name derives from the Hebrew word negev, meaning south. The Negev has long been Israel's southern frontier. It receives between one and eight inches of rainfall annually, depending on elevation. The northern Negev is marginally less arid than the southern portions.

The Negev is home to the Dead Sea, the world's lowest land elevation at approximately one thousand four hundred ten feet below sea level, and to salt deposits of significant economic value. Bedouin communities have herded sheep and camels in the Negev for centuries. Their traditional settlement patterns and land tenure have been complicated by Israeli state consolidation.

The Ramon Crater, also known as Makhtesh Ramon, is one of the world's largest erosion craters, offering striking geological formations and serving as a major tourist destination. Ancient Nabataean cities like Avdat and Mampsis flourished in the Negev as trading hubs on the spice routes connecting Arabia to the Mediterranean.

Modern Israeli development has included irrigation agriculture, kibbutzim, moshavim, and industrial cities. The Negev is now slated for major population expansion. The region remains geographically and culturally linked to the broader arid Levant. The Dead Sea contains the lowest point in the Negev and the surrounding region, while Bedouin pastoral societies and Nabataean trading empires speak to the deep history of settlement and commerce.
